spoken: In 1874, the English economist William Stanley Jevons printed this puzzle.
Which two numbers, multiplied together, make 8,616,460,799?
I think it unlikely, he wrote, that anyone but myself will ever know.
Multiplying two numbers is easy. Finding them again from the answer can be very hard.
Lopsided problems like his now guard every secure web page you open.
They let two strangers agree on a secret while everyone listens.
This is the story of public-key cryptography, which was invented twice.
For most of history, sending a secret message meant sharing a secret key first.
The same key locks and unlocks the message, so whoever has it can read everything.
So the key had to travel, by trusted courier or at a face-to-face meeting.
And every pair of people who want to talk privately needs its own key.
Ten people need 45 keys.
A thousand people need 499,500.
Two researchers at Stanford called this the key distribution problem in 1976.
Their answer sounds impossible. It lets strangers agree on a key in full view of everyone.
In 1974, Whitfield Diffie, an independent researcher, was advised to meet a young Stanford professor, Martin Hellman.
A planned half-hour meeting lasted many hours.
In November 1976, they published New Directions in Cryptography.
Its first line reads, We stand today on the brink of a revolution in cryptography.
The big idea was to split the key in two.
One key locks, a different key unlocks, and knowing the first doesn't give you the second.
Publish your locking key like a phone number, and anyone can send you messages only you can read.
For that they needed a trapdoor one-way function, which is easy to compute but hard to undo, unless you hold a secret.
They didn't have one. The problem, they wrote, was still largely open.
But they did have a way to agree on a key in public, building on ideas from Ralph Merkle.
Here's the idea in paint. Alice and Bob publicly agree on yellow as their starting colour.
Each mixes in a secret colour of their own, red for Alice and blue for Bob.
They swap the mixtures in the open, where Eve, listening in, sees them too.
Then each stirs in their own secret again, and both end up with the same brown.
Eve has the yellow and both mixtures, but she can't pull the secret colours back out.
Here the picture breaks down. Paint can never be unmixed, but the maths can, by trying every secret.
The defence is sheer numbers, with far too many secrets to try.
The real thing uses clock arithmetic. Picture a clock with 23 hours.
Start at 1 and keep multiplying by 5, keeping only the remainder after dividing by 23.
The hand jumps to 5, then 2, then 10, then 4, then 20, with no pattern you can easily see.
Stepping forward is easy. Working back to how many steps it took is the discrete logarithm problem, and it's hard.
Now comes the exchange. Everyone, Eve included, knows 23 and 5.
Alice secretly picks 3. After 3 steps, the hand is on 10, and she sends 10.
Bob secretly picks 7. After 7 steps, the hand is on 17, and he sends 17.
Alice raises Bob's 17 to the power of her secret 3, and Bob raises Alice's 10 to the power of his 7.
Both get 14, because both have really taken 3 times 7 steps from the start, which is 21.
Eve heard the numbers 23 and 5, then 10 and 17. To reach 14, she needs 3 or 7.
With 23 hours she could try them all, so real exchanges use a prime of at least 2,048 bits, which is 617 digits.
But a true public lock, one that anyone could close, was still missing.
At M I T, Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman spent about a year hunting for one.
Rivest and Shamir proposed ideas, and Adleman, the mathematician, kept breaking them.
In April 1977, after a Passover evening at a student's house, Rivest couldn't sleep.
By daybreak, the story goes, he had much of the paper written.
The method, named R S A after their initials, starts with two primes.
Let's build a tiny key. Take the primes 61 and 53, and multiply them to get 3,233.
Pick 17 as the power that locks. From the primes, we can work out that the power that unlocks is 413.
The public key is just 3,233 and 17. Anyone can have it.
To send Bob 65, raise it to the power of 17 and keep the remainder after dividing by 3,233.
That power has 31 digits, but only the remainder, 2,790, travels.
Bob raises that to the power of 413, divides by 3,233 again, and out comes 65.
Finding 413 needs the two primes, and the public key shows only their product.
Real systems also add random padding. Bare R S A like this is just a demonstration.
It all rests on a lopsided pair of jobs. Multiplying is easy, and factoring is hard.
To factor 3,233, try dividing by each prime in turn. The 16th prime, which is 53, works.
Jevons's number needs thousands of tries. It's 89,681 times 96,079.
Charles Busk found that in 1889.
In August 1977, Martin Gardner described R S A in Scientific American, along with a challenge message locked with a 129 digit number.
Rivest estimated that, with the best methods of the day, a 125 digit number would take 40 quadrillion years.
But better methods came, and about 600 volunteers, with some 1,600 computers, cracked it in 1994.
The message read, the magic words are squeamish ossifrage.
So keys grew. Public factoring records are under 300 digits. A 2,048 bit key has 617.
And no one has proved that factoring is hard. There's just no fast way known on ordinary computers.
Run the same maths the other way, and you get something just as useful, which is a signature.
Diffie and Hellman proposed digital signatures in 1976, and R S A made them work.
Bob locks a message with his private 413. Anyone can open it with his public 17.
Signing 1977 gives 788, and raising 788 to the power of 17 gives back 1977.
Only the holder of 413 could have made 788, so it proves who signed.
In practice you sign a short fingerprint of the message, called a hash.
Signatures also close a gap in key exchange, one that lets an attacker sit in the middle.
Mallory sits between Alice and Bob and runs one exchange with each, posing as the other.
Each thinks they share a key with the other. Both share one with Mallory, who reads everything.
Plain Diffie–Hellman can't tell who is really on the other end.
On the web, the proof is a certificate, which is the site's public key, signed by an authority your browser trusts.
There's a twist, kept secret for more than twenty years.
In January 1970, at Britain's G C H Q, James Ellis wrote a secret report on non-secret encryption.
The idea came from a wartime Bell Labs paper, in which the receiver adds noise to a call, then removes it.
Ellis argued that it was possible, but he couldn't see a way to build it.
In September 1973, a young mathematician, Clifford Cocks, joined and heard about the idea.
Cocks knew number theory. He chose prime factoring, and quickly found what we now call R S A.
He didn't even write it down at the time.
In 1974, his colleague Malcolm Williamson found what we now call Diffie–Hellman key exchange.
With a military focus and little computing power, G C H Q found no use for it, and it stayed secret.
It was made public in 1997, when Cocks gave a talk on the 18th of December.
James Ellis had died on the 25th of November, a month too soon.
As far as anyone knows, the Stanford and M I T teams found it all on their own.
So what happens when you open a secure web page today?
Your browser and the server run a fresh key exchange, often on elliptic curves rather than a clock.
The server signs the exchange, and its certificate shows that the signature really is the site's.
Public-key maths is slow, so it only sets up a key; a fast ordinary cipher carries the page.
The exchange keys are thrown away afterwards, so a key stolen later can't unlock today's traffic.
R S A keys usually have 2,048 bits or more. On elliptic curves, 256 bits does as well as 3,072.
In 1994, Peter Shor showed how a quantum computer could factor huge numbers quickly.
It solves discrete logarithms too, so it would break R S A and Diffie–Hellman alike.
No such machine exists yet. Demonstrations have factored only 15 and 21, helped by knowing the answer.
Breaking real keys might take millions of qubits, because of error correction.
But a message recorded today could be decrypted later. This is called harvest now, decrypt later.
In August 2024, N I S T, the U S standards institute, published three post-quantum standards, one for keys and two for signatures.
The key one, M L Kem, rests on lattice problems, which are thought to resist quantum attacks.
Chrome and Firefox already mix it into their key exchange, alongside a classic elliptic curve.
So strangers can agree on a key in public, because some sums are easy one way and hard the other.
A lock can be public, if only its owner knows the trapdoor.
And run backwards, the same maths signs.
Jevons was wrong about his number, but right that some sums are far easier done than undone.
Every secure connection begins that way, with two strangers, in public, agreeing on a secret only they know.
